claim: Rai14 is an F-actin-regulating protein with six ankyrin repeats and coiled-coil structures.
source: Retinoic acid-induced protein 14 (Rai14) is a filamentous actin (F-actin) regulating protein with six ankyrin repeats and coiled-coil structures (Kutty et al., 2001; Peng et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Kutty et al., 2001; Peng et al., 2000).

claim: Rai14 confers integrity of actin filament bundles in several tissues.
source: Functional studies on Rai14 illustrated its role in conferring integrity of actin filament bundles in several tissues (Qian et al., 2013a; Qian et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Qian et al., 2013a; Qian et al., 2013b).

claim: Rai14 has membrane-shaping capability and affects dendritic branch formation.
source: Recently, it was reported that Rai14 has membrane-shaping capability and affects dendritic branch formation (Wolf et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Wolf et al., 2019).

claim: Rai14 homozygous knockout (Rai14-/-) mice showed perinatal lethality.
source: Since Rai14 homozygous knockout (Rai14-/-) mice showed perinatal lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), Rai14 heterozygous knockout (Rai14+/-) mice were used for the in vivo experiments and behavioral analyses.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 which shows genotype distributions and morphology of Rai14-deficient embryos.

claim: Rai14-deficient neurons in mouse cortex displayed a significantly lower number of dendritic spines than wild-type neurons.
source: Rai14-deficient neurons in mouse cortex and hippocampus displayed a significantly lower number of dendritic spines than wild-type neurons (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B, which includes representative images and quantitative analysis of dendritic spine density.

claim: Rai14-deficient neurons in mouse hippocampus displayed a significantly lower number of dendritic spines than wild-type neurons.
source: Rai14-deficient neurons in mouse cortex and hippocampus displayed a significantly lower number of dendritic spines than wild-type neurons (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B, which includes representative images and quantitative analysis of dendritic spine density.

claim: Primary cultured hippocampal neurons from Rai14-/- embryos showed significantly lower dendritic spine density.
source: Primary cultured hippocampal neurons from Rai14-/- embryos showed significantly lower dendritic spine density (Figure 1C and D) without significant differences in spine length or spine head size (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D, which includes representative images and quantitative analysis of dendritic spine density.

claim: Rai14-/- neurons showed no significant differences in spine length compared to wild-type neurons.
source: Primary cultured hippocampal neurons from Rai14-/- embryos showed significantly lower dendritic spine density (Figure 1C and D) without significant differences in spine length or spine head size (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E, which includes cumulative probability plots of spine length.

claim: Rai14-/- neurons showed no significant differences in spine head size compared to wild-type neurons.
source: Primary cultured hippocampal neurons from Rai14-/- embryos showed significantly lower dendritic spine density (Figure 1C and D) without significant differences in spine length or spine head size (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E, which includes cumulative probability plots of maximal diameter of spine head width.

claim: Knockdown of Rai14 in primary cortical neurons reduced the numbers of dendritic spines.
source: Similarly, knockdown of Rai14 in primary cortical and hippocampal neurons (Figure 1F and G) and P14 mouse cortical neurons (Figure 1H) reduced the numbers of dendritic spines, indicating that the loss of dendritic spines upon Rai14 downregulation is cell-autonomous.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F, which includes representative images and quantitative analysis of dendritic spine density in cortical neurons expressing Rai14 shRNA.

claim: Knockdown of Rai14 in primary hippocampal neurons reduced the numbers of dendritic spines.
source: Similarly, knockdown of Rai14 in primary cortical and hippocampal neurons (Figure 1F and G) and P14 mouse cortical neurons (Figure 1H) reduced the numbers of dendritic spines, indicating that the loss of dendritic spines upon Rai14 downregulation is cell-autonomous.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G, which includes representative images and quantitative analysis of dendritic spine density in hippocampal neurons expressing Rai14 shRNA.

claim: Knockdown of Rai14 in P14 mouse cortical neurons reduced the numbers of dendritic spines.
source: Similarly, knockdown of Rai14 in primary cortical and hippocampal neurons (Figure 1F and G) and P14 mouse cortical neurons (Figure 1H) reduced the numbers of dendritic spines, indicating that the loss of dendritic spines upon Rai14 downregulation is cell-autonomous.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H, which includes representative images and quantitative analysis of dendritic spine density in P14 mouse cortical neurons expressing Rai14 shRNA.

claim: The loss of dendritic spines upon Rai14 downregulation is cell-autonomous.
source: Similarly, knockdown of Rai14 in primary cortical and hippocampal neurons (Figure 1F and G) and P14 mouse cortical neurons (Figure 1H) reduced the numbers of dendritic spines, indicating that the loss of dendritic spines upon Rai14 downregulation is cell-autonomous.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Rai14 knockdown in different neuronal preparations consistently reduces spine density.

claim: Rai14 and Tara share multiple interaction partners.
source: Rai14 and Tara share multiple additional interaction partners (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that they likely form a functional complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, which shows a protein interactome image from BioPlex.

claim: Rai14 and Tara likely form a functional complex.
source: Rai14 and Tara share multiple additional interaction partners (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that they likely form a functional complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Rai14 and Tara share multiple interaction partners.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid screening using a human fetal brain cDNA library validated the interaction between Rai14 and Tara.
source: Indeed, a yeast two-hybrid screening using a human fetal brain cDNA library validated this interaction (Figure 2A), which was also confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of Rai14 and Tara from mouse brain lysates (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, which shows yeast two-hybrid assay results.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of Rai14 and Tara from mouse brain lysates confirmed their interaction.
source: Indeed, a yeast two-hybrid screening using a human fetal brain cDNA library validated this interaction (Figure 2A), which was also confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of Rai14 and Tara from mouse brain lysates (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, which shows co-immunoprecipitation results.

claim: Knockdown of Tara led to the downregulation of Rai14 protein levels.
source: Notably, knockdown of Tara led to the downregulation of Rai14 protein levels (Figure 2C), whereas overexpression of Tara brought about the upregulation of endogenous Rai14 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, which shows western blot images and quantification of Rai14 levels upon Tara knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of Tara brought about the upregulation of endogenous Rai14 protein levels.
source: Notably, knockdown of Tara led to the downregulation of Rai14 protein levels (Figure 2C), whereas overexpression of Tara brought about the upregulation of endogenous Rai14 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, which shows western blot images and quantification of Rai14 levels upon Tara overexpression.

claim: Tara knockdown resulted in a reduction in dendritic spine density similar to Rai14 shRNA.
source: Tara knockdown resulted in a similar reduction in dendritic spine density to those expressing Rai14 shRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, which shows quantification of dendritic spine density under different knockdown conditions.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of Rai14 and Tara decreased spine density to a similar extent as single knockdowns.
source: In addition, the simultaneous knockdown of Rai14 and Tara also decreased spine density to a similar extent.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, which shows quantification of dendritic spine density under double knockdown conditions.

claim: The TaraΔ241–330 mutant, lacking the region for Rai14 binding, failed to upregulate Rai14.
source: The TaraΔ241–330 mutant, lacking the region for Rai14 binding, failed to upregulate Rai14, whereas a fragment of Tara (aa 241–330) harboring the Rai14-binding region was sufficient to stabilize Rai14, indicating that Rai14 is stabilized by physical associations with Tara (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F, which shows western blot images and quantification of Rai14 levels with different Tara constructs.

claim: A fragment of Tara (aa 241–330) harboring the Rai14-binding region was sufficient to stabilize Rai14.
source: The TaraΔ241–330 mutant, lacking the region for Rai14 binding, failed to upregulate Rai14, whereas a fragment of Tara (aa 241–330) harboring the Rai14-binding region was sufficient to stabilize Rai14, indicating that Rai14 is stabilized by physical associations with Tara (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F, which shows western blot images and quantification of Rai14 levels with different Tara constructs.

claim: Rai14 is stabilized by physical associations with Tara.
source: The TaraΔ241–330 mutant, lacking the region for Rai14 binding, failed to upregulate Rai14, whereas a fragment of Tara (aa 241–330) harboring the Rai14-binding region was sufficient to stabilize Rai14, indicating that Rai14 is stabilized by physical associations with Tara (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Tara binding is necessary and sufficient for Rai14 upregulation.

claim: The tip of the carboxyl-terminal region of Rai14 contains multiple typical protein degradation motifs.
source: The binding interface was localized to the tip of the carboxyl-terminal region containing multiple typical protein degradation motifs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C, which shows predicted protease cleavage sites in the Rai14 sequence.

claim: A Rai14 mutant lacking the motifs in aa 948–967, Rai14Δ948–967, showed significantly elevated protein levels regardless of Tara co-expression.
source: Indeed, a Rai14 mutant lacking the motifs in aa 948–967, Rai14Δ948–967, showed significantly elevated protein levels regardless of Tara co-expression (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, which shows western blot images and quantification of Rai14 mutant levels.

claim: Rai14Δ948–967 lost capacity to interact with Tara.
source: As this mutant also lost capacity to interact with Tara (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), it is likely that Tara stabilizes Rai14 by interfering with its degradation motifs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, which shows co-immunoprecipitation results.

claim: Tara stabilizes Rai14 by interfering with its degradation motifs.
source: As this mutant also lost capacity to interact with Tara (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), it is likely that Tara stabilizes Rai14 by interfering with its degradation motifs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of degradation motifs stabilizes Rai14 and abolishes Tara interaction.

claim: Co-expression of Rai14 and Tara resulted in increased spine density.
source: The co-expression of Rai14 and Tara, which led to Rai14 upregulation, resulted in increased spine density, whereas the co-expression of Rai14 and TaraΔ241–330 failed to increase dendritic spine density (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H, which shows representative images and quantification of dendritic spine density.

claim: Co-expression of Rai14 and TaraΔ241–330 failed to increase dendritic spine density.
source: The co-expression of Rai14 and Tara, which led to Rai14 upregulation, resulted in increased spine density, whereas the co-expression of Rai14 and TaraΔ241–330 failed to increase dendritic spine density (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H, which shows representative images and quantification of dendritic spine density.

claim: Expression of Rai14Δ948–967 alone was sufficient to increase spine density.
source: Moreover, unlike wild-type Rai14, the expression of Rai14Δ948–967, a stabilized form of Rai14, alone was sufficient to increase spine density (Figure 2I), further supporting the hypothesis that Tara stabilizes Rai14 by physical interaction to positively regulate dendritic spine density.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I, which shows representative images and quantification of dendritic spine density.

claim: Tara stabilizes Rai14 by physical interaction to positively regulate dendritic spine density.
source: Moreover, unlike wild-type Rai14, the expression of Rai14Δ948–967, a stabilized form of Rai14, alone was sufficient to increase spine density (Figure 2I), further supporting the hypothesis that Tara stabilizes Rai14 by physical interaction to positively regulate dendritic spine density.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that stabilized Rai14 increases spine density without Tara.

claim: Co-expression of Rai14 and Tara remarkably enhanced the intensity of Rai14 compared to ectopically expressed Rai14 without co-expression of Tara.
source: Consistently, co-expression of Rai14 and Tara remarkably enhanced the intensity of Rai14 compared to ectopically expressed Rai14 without co-expression of Tara (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, which shows localization and intensity of Rai14 in neurons.

claim: When Tara was co-expressed, both Tara and Rai14 displayed a strong tendency to cluster at the neck and/or base of the dendritic spines.
source: Interestingly, when Tara was co-expressed, both Tara and Rai14 displayed a strong tendency to cluster at the neck and/or base of the dendritic spines (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B, which shows localization and quantification of Rai14 clusters at spine necks.

claim: Rai14Δ948–967 accumulated at the neck of some spines without Tara co-expression.

claim: When Rai14ΔANK was co-expressed with Tara, it did not exhibit selective accumulation at the neck of dendritic spines.

claim: Rai14ΔANK lacked membrane-binding ability.

claim: Rai14Δ948–967 effectively enhanced spine density.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, which shows quantification of dendritic spine density with different Rai14 constructs.

claim: Rai14ΔANK failed to increase dendritic spine density compared to Rai14 and Tara co-expressing dendrites.
source: The accumulation of the stabilized Rai14 at the spine neck was in a tight correlation with dendritic spine density (Figure 3C); Rai14Δ948–967 effectively enhanced spine density whereas Rai14ΔANK, which was able to interact with and was upregulated by Tara (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), failed to increase dendritic spine density compared to Rai14 and Tara co-expressing dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, which shows quantification of dendritic spine density with different Rai14 constructs.

claim: Rai14ΔANK was able to interact with and was upregulated by Tara.
source: The accumulation of the stabilized Rai14 at the spine neck was in a tight correlation with dendritic spine density (Figure 3C); Rai14Δ948–967 effectively enhanced spine density whereas Rai14ΔANK, which was able to interact with and was upregulated by Tara (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), failed to increase dendritic spine density compared to Rai14 and Tara co-expressing dendrites.

claim: The fraction of eliminated spines was markedly decreased in the Rai14-positive spines.

claim: Rai14 sometimes gathered at the base and entered the neck of newly formed dendritic spines.
source: Rai14 sometimes gathered at the base and entered the neck of newly formed dendritic spines (Figure 3F).

claim: Newly formed Rai14-negative spines shrank or disappeared.

claim: Dendritic spines with ectopic expression of Rai14 and Tara showed significantly higher survival rates against LatA treatment than controls.
source: Dendritic spines with ectopic expression of Rai14 and Tara showed significantly higher survival rates against LatA treatment than controls, indicating that Rai14 protects dendritic spines from the pressure of elimination by actin destabilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and H, which shows normalized spine density and fractions of eliminated/newly formed spines after LatA treatment.

claim: Rai14 protects dendritic spines from the pressure of elimination by actin destabilization.
source: Dendritic spines with ectopic expression of Rai14 and Tara showed significantly higher survival rates against LatA treatment than controls, indicating that Rai14 protects dendritic spines from the pressure of elimination by actin destabilization.

claim: The Rai14-Tara complex helps in the maintenance of dendritic spines.
source: Collectively, these data support that the Rai14-Tara complex helps in the maintenance of dendritic spines.

claim: Neurons co-expressing Rai14 and Tara displayed more spines with both synaptophysin and PSD95 puncta on the spine head compared to control neurons.

claim: Within Rai14-Tara overexpressing neurons, spines containing the Rai14 cluster tended to bear synapses with higher probability than the spines without Rai14 signal.

claim: Rai14-/- neurons had less number of spines marked simultaneously with synaptophysin and PSD95 puncta on the spine head than wild-type neurons.

claim: mEPSCs measured from acute brain slices of Rai14+/- mice showed significantly lower mean frequency without alteration of the amplitude.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–G, which shows representative mEPSC traces and quantification of frequency and amplitude.

claim: Rai14+/- mice stayed significantly less in the platform-containing quadrant in the Morris water maze probe test.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H–K, which shows experimental scheme, trajectories, and quantification of Morris water maze test results.

claim: Wild-type littermates spent more time in the platform area in the Morris water maze probe test.

claim: Rai14+/- mice displayed mild deficits in contextual fear memory without fear generalization.

claim: The structural deficits in spine maintenance caused by Rai14 deficiency extend to functional alterations in synapses.

claim: 17 genes out of 18 significant DEGs that are included in the Aston-Major Depressive Disorder DN gene set were downregulated in Rai14+/- mouse brain.
